About Me

I am a molecular biologist with a great affinity for coding. Over the years, I gained expertise in the fields of single-cell omics, spatial technologies, bioinformatics, and advanced fluorescence imaging. I thus bring a hybrid profile with both wet-lab and computational experience.


During my Ph.D. at the University of Cambridge, I embarked on a collaborative project to generate one of the first single-cell transcriptomic atlases delineating cell type diversification during early mouse development (Pijuan-Sala et al., Nature, 2019), and I led independently a project to characterize developmental chromatin accessibility states using single-nucleus ATAC-seq ( Pijuan-Sala et al., Nature Cell Biology, 2020). Working at a time when single-cell omics methods were still emerging meant learning to solve many problems from first principles, which shaped my approach to computational analysis and bioinformatics.


In my postdoctoral work at EMBL, I moved toward a more experimental role with the aim of contributing to the development and establishment of emerging spatial imaging technologies in multicellular organisms, using Drosophila embryos as a model system. This experience highlighted the practical challenges of building methods in a nascent field - breaking complex problems into tractable steps, planning for contingencies, and appreciating the importance of thoughtful project and time management. Alongside this work, I developed custom image-analysis pipelines to analyse the resulting data.


What motivates me is developing new strategies to tackle biological problems. I am particularly drawn to the technical and engineering aspects of science: thinking creatively, troubleshooting collaboratively, and integrating tools across disciplines. I value team-oriented environments with clear shared objectives, where individual contributions are well defined and recognised.


Looking ahead, I am eager to translate and further expand my computational expertise in a more translational setting, with a particular interest in cancer biology.
